title: Golden Gate Bridge by Bike, to Sausalito
summary: Ride the flat bayside path from Fisherman's Wharf past Fort Mason, the Marina and Crissy Field, cross the Golden Gate Bridge, and roll down to Sausalito to catch the ferry back.
intro: Welcome to San Francisco! I'm your guide for a bike ride of about three hours, stops included. We'll follow the bay west to the Golden Gate Bridge, ride across it, and coast down to the little town of Sausalito, where you can take the ferry back. First, a few safety rules. Wear one earbud only, or use your phone's speaker, so you can always hear traffic and other riders. Never touch your phone while you're riding. You don't need to: each story starts on its own when you reach the right spot. If you want to look around, pull over somewhere safe first. Bring a jacket, because it gets windy and cold on the bridge. Ready? Let's ride.

stops.name: Aquatic Park
stops.text: You're at Aquatic Park, a small sandy cove right next to Fisherman's Wharf. That white building that looks like an ocean liner is the old Bathhouse, built in the late nineteen thirties as a public works project during the Great Depression. Today it's part of the San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park. Look out at the water. You may see swimmers in the cove, even in winter, with no wetsuits. Two local swimming and rowing clubs have been here for well over a century. To your right, the tall masts belong to the historic ships at Hyde Street Pier. Now, this promenade is for people on foot, so walk your bike west along it, past the Bathhouse, to the end of Van Ness Avenue, where a long pier curves out into the bay.

stops.name: To the Municipal Pier
stops.text: This long curving pier is the Municipal Pier. It wraps around the cove like an arm and shelters the swimmers from the open bay. Locals come out here to fish and to watch the sunset. From here, get back on your bike and follow the bike path uphill into Fort Mason. It's a short climb, and it's fine to walk if you need to.

stops.name: Fort Mason
stops.text: Welcome to Fort Mason. This hill has been a military site for a long time. The Spanish put a small gun battery near here in the seventeen nineties, and the United States Army took it over in the eighteen sixties. During the Second World War, Fort Mason was the army's port for the Pacific, and well over a million soldiers shipped out from the piers below. Today it's all parkland and an arts center, part of the Golden Gate National Recreation Area. The big lawn is called the Great Meadow. Look out for the statue of Phillip Burton, the congressman who fought to create this park. Now follow the path downhill to Marina Boulevard, then ride west, keeping the water on your right.
stops.credit: Brocken Inaglory, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Marina Green
stops.text: This long lawn is the Marina Green, famous for kite flyers, joggers and some of the best views in the city. On a clear day you can see the Golden Gate Bridge ahead and Alcatraz out to your right. Here's the surprise: much of the land under you used to be water and marsh. It was filled in for the Panama Pacific International Exposition of nineteen fifteen, a world's fair that celebrated the new Panama Canal and the city's rebirth after the nineteen oh six earthquake. Filled land shakes hard, and in the earthquake of nineteen eighty nine, this neighborhood was badly damaged. Out on the jetty past the harbor there's the Wave Organ, a sculpture that lets you hear the waves. Keep riding west, then follow the signs left to the Palace of Fine Arts.
stops.credit: Guillaume Paumier, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Palace of Fine Arts
stops.text: This is the Palace of Fine Arts, the grandest survivor of the nineteen fifteen world's fair. It was designed by the architect Bernard Maybeck to look like a Roman ruin reflected in a lagoon. Like the rest of the fair, it was meant to be temporary, built of plaster over a wooden frame. But San Franciscans loved it so much that they saved it, and in the nineteen sixties it was rebuilt in concrete. Look up at the top of the colonnade. Those women with their backs to you, leaning on big boxes, are often called the weeping women. Watch for swans and ducks on the lagoon. Walk your bike on these paths. When you're done, head back up toward the bay and pick up the path into Crissy Field.

stops.name: Into Crissy Field
stops.text: You're now entering Crissy Field. Stay on the wide gravel and paved path along the beach, and keep to the right, because this path is shared with walkers, runners and dogs. The bridge is straight ahead of you now, getting bigger with every minute. The bay is often windy here, so you may see kite surfers and windsurfers out on the water.

stops.name: Crissy Field
stops.text: A hundred years ago, this was an army airfield. It was named after Major Dana Crissy, a pilot who died in nineteen nineteen during a cross country air race. Planes took off from this strip of land in the early days of flight, but strong winds and fog made it a tricky place to fly, and later the land was covered in asphalt and old buildings. Then, around the year two thousand, it was turned back into a park. Thousands of volunteers helped plant native plants, and the tidal marsh you see was brought back to life. Birds came back too, and herons and egrets now hunt in the marsh you just passed. Keep riding west along the shore toward the bridge.
stops.credit: Frank Schulenburg, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Past the Warming Hut
stops.text: That small building on your left is the Warming Hut, a café and shop, and the last easy stop for a coffee or a snack before the bridge. Across from it, on the water side, is a fishing pier. Keep going straight along the water to the very end of the road, right under the bridge. On big swell days you may spot surfers riding waves near the old fort.

stops.name: Fort Point
stops.text: Stop here and look up. You're right under the Golden Gate Bridge. The brick fort in front of you is Fort Point, built by the army between eighteen fifty three and eighteen sixty one, during the Gold Rush, to guard the entrance to the bay. It was built for more than a hundred cannons, yet it never fired a shot in battle. When the bridge was planned in the nineteen thirties, the chief engineer, Joseph Strauss, decided to save the fort, so his team designed a special steel arch to pass right over it. You can see it above you. Movie fans may know this spot from Alfred Hitchcock's Vertigo. Now ride back the way you came, and follow the bike signs uphill to the bridge plaza. It's steep, so walk if you like.
stops.credit: Brocken Inaglory, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Golden Gate Bridge Welcome Center
stops.text: Made it up the hill! This is the bridge plaza, with the Welcome Center, a café and restrooms. Look for the statue of Joseph Strauss, the chief engineer. Nearby there's a cut piece of one of the bridge's main cables. Each main cable is almost a meter thick, and it's made of more than twenty seven thousand thin steel wires bundled together. Those two cables hold up the whole road deck. If it's foggy, listen for the foghorns. Now get ready to cross. Bikes share the sidewalk with people on foot. Signs at the entrance tell you which side bikes use, and it can change with the day and the time. Ride slowly, ring your bell, and give way to walkers.
stops.credit: Brocken Inaglory, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Onto the bridge
stops.text: You're on the bridge now. Stay on the bike side, keep your speed down and both hands on the handlebars. The wind can push you hard here, so hold your line. Ahead of you is the south tower. It rises about two hundred and twenty seven meters above the water, as tall as a sixty or seventy story building. Ride on, and I'll tell you the bridge's story along the way.

stops.name: Middle of the bridge
stops.text: Keep rolling and listen. If you want to look, stop only where you're fully out of the way. Building this bridge was a huge risk. Many experts said the strait was too deep, too windy and too foggy. Work started in January nineteen thirty three, and the bridge opened in May nineteen thirty seven, when about two hundred thousand people walked across on opening day. For more than twenty five years, it had the longest main span of any suspension bridge in the world. A safety net under the deck saved the lives of nineteen workers, who called themselves the Halfway to Hell Club, but eleven men died. And the color? It's called International Orange. It was chosen because it blends with the hills and stands out in the fog. Keep riding to the north end, then follow the signs to Vista Point.

stops.name: Vista Point
stops.text: You've crossed the Golden Gate! This is Vista Point, and that's the classic view: the bridge, the city skyline, and Alcatraz out in the bay. The name Golden Gate is older than the bridge, and even older than the Gold Rush. An American explorer, John Frémont, named this narrow strait in eighteen forty six, after the Golden Horn of Istanbul. The green hills around you are the Marin Headlands. They're dotted with old army batteries and bunkers, and they stayed wild partly because the army kept them closed for so long. In summer, watch the fog pour in from the ocean and flow under the bridge. When you're ready, follow the bike signs to Alexander Avenue and head downhill toward Sausalito.

stops.name: Down Alexander Avenue
stops.text: This is a long, fast downhill, so control your speed and keep your hands near the brakes. Stay to the right, because cars use this road too. Below you, down by the water, is Fort Baker, another old army post. Today its old officers' homes are a hotel and a park. At the bottom, follow the road into Sausalito.

stops.name: Sausalito waterfront
stops.text: Welcome to Sausalito. The name comes from Spanish and is usually translated as little willow grove. Look back across the water. San Francisco is right there, but this feels like a different world. During the Second World War, a huge shipyard called Marinship was built at the north end of town, and workers there built nearly a hundred ships in just a few years. After the war, some people moved onto old boats and barges near the shipyard, and that's how Sausalito's famous houseboat community began. Artists and musicians followed. Keep riding slowly along Bridgeway, the main street by the water, toward downtown and the ferry terminal.

stops.name: Sausalito ferry terminal
stops.text: You made it! This is the Sausalito ferry terminal, the end of our ride. Two ferry companies sail back to San Francisco from here. One goes to the Ferry Building downtown, and the other goes to the piers near Fisherman's Wharf, closer to where we started and to many bike rental shops. Ferry times vary, and bike space on board is limited, so check the schedule and get in line early, especially on sunny afternoons. Before you board, take a break. Grab something to eat, walk along the water, and enjoy the view of the city you just rode out of. Thanks for riding with me. Enjoy the trip back across the bay.
